prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current methods for comparing neural image representations (both artificial and biological) typically rely on measures of global geometric similarity. However, models that appear globally similar often exhibit drastically different behaviors in their "local" geometry—specifically, how their internal representations shift in response to minute, imperceptible perturbations of the input (as seen in adversarial examples).

Existing tools for probing these local discrepancies are severely limited in scale. Current approaches can generally only characterize a single model (identifying its own most-noticeable distortions) or optimally distinguish between a single pair of models. There is currently no principled, scalable framework for selecting the optimal input stimuli to differentiate a large collection of $N$ models simultaneously. This prevents efficient large-scale comparison of diverse architectures and limits our ability to select the most informative stimuli for psychophysical comparisons with human perception.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can generalize the comparison of local model geometries by treating the sensitivity profiles of different models as points in a metric space. By defining a distance metric based on the disagreement in sensitivity between models, we propose that we can identify "Principal Distortions"—specific directions in the input space that maximize the variance of model responses.

Analogous to how Principal Component Analysis (PCA) finds directions of maximum variance in a dataset, we believe we can synthesize specific image distortions that act as the "axes" of maximum disagreement across a population of models. This will allow us to reduce the high-dimensional space of possible image perturbations down to a few critical directions that best separate the local geometries of the entire model set.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose to develop a computational framework that operates on the local differential structure of image representations. The approach will follow these logical steps:

1.  **Quantifying Local Sensitivity via Fisher Information:**
    We will characterize the local geometry of each model using the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM). We will treat models as stochastic mapping functions (assuming additive noise for deterministic models). The FIM will allow us to mathematically define how distinct a perturbed input is from a base input from the perspective of the model’s internal representation.

2.  **Defining a Relative Sensitivity Metric:**
    We will construct a pairwise metric to compare any two models. This metric will measure the "distance" between their local geometries by looking at the log-ratio of their sensitivities to a specific distortion vector. Crucially, we will design this metric to be invariant to the arbitrary scaling of model responses, ensuring we capture geometric shape differences rather than magnitude differences.

3.  **Optimization for Principal Distortions:**
    To handle $N$ models simultaneously, we will formulate an optimization objective that seeks to maximize the spread (variance) of the models under our defined metric.
    *   We will define an objective function that aggregates the pairwise distances between all models in the set for a given distortion.
    *   We will use gradient-based optimization (projected gradient descent) to synthesize specific distortion vectors (images) that maximize this objective.
    *   These optimized vectors will be the "Principal Distortions"—the specific inputs that cause the models’ sensitivity ratios to diverge the most.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Theoretical Framework:** A generalized metric space for comparing the local information geometry of an arbitrary number of stochastic representations, overcoming the binary limitation of previous methods.
2.  **Scalable Model Comparison:** An automated method to "judiciously select" the most informative stimuli for differentiating complex models. This effectively acts as a dimensionality reduction technique for representational geometry.
3.  **Experimental Efficiency:** By synthesizing the stimuli that maximally separate model behaviors, we will enable more efficient psychophysical experiments. Researchers will be able to rank models against human perception using a minimal set of highly informative images, rather than relying on large-scale brute-force testing.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

### Hardware and Software
*   **Hardware:** Computations were performed on NVIDIA GPUs (RTX A6000 and A100 models).
*   **Software Framework:** Models were implemented in PyTorch. Deep neural networks utilized the `timm` (PyTorch Image Models) library and `plenoptic`.

### Models
**1. Early Visual Models:**
*   **Type:** Nested family of deterministic models designed to capture early primate visual system properties (LGN).
*   **Variants:**
    *   **LN:** Linear-Nonlinear (removes contrast and luminance gain control).
    *   **LG:** Linear-Gain (removes contrast gain control).
    *   **LGG:** Linear-Gain-Gain (removes OFF channel).
    *   **LGN:** Full model (ON/OFF channels, rectification, luminance and contrast gain control).
*   **Parameterization:** Parameters were fixed to values previously fit to human distortion ratings from the TID-2008 database (see Raw Numeric Data section).
*   **Noise Assumption:** Output assumed to be corrupted by additive Gaussian noise to calculate the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM).

**2. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs):**
*   **Standard Models:** AlexNet and ResNet50 (pre-trained on ImageNet-1k).
*   **Texture-Bias Models:** AlexNet and ResNet50 trained on Stylized ImageNet (SIN).
*   **Adversarially Trained (AT) Models:**
    *   ResNet50: $\ell_2$ robustness ($\epsilon_{train} = 3.0$).
    *   AlexNet: $\ell_2$ robustness ($\epsilon_{train} = 3.0$).
*   **Modern Architectures:**
    *   EfficientNet-B0 (trained on ImageNet-1k, $224 \times 224$).
    *   ViT (Base-Patch16-224) (trained on ImageNet-1k).
*   **Layer Selection:** Only intermediate layers before the final classification stage were analyzed.
    *   *AlexNet Layers:* relu0, relu1, relu2, relu3, relu4, fc0_relu, fc1_relu.
    *   *ResNet50 Layers:* conv1_relu1, layer1, layer2, layer3, layer4, avgpool.

### Datasets
*   **Early Visual Model Experiments:** Images from the Kodak TID 2008 dataset.
*   **DNN Main Experiments:** A subset of 100 ImageNet images, each from a unique class.
*   **Foreground/Background Blur Experiments:** ImageNet-9 dataset with foreground/background masks. 72 total images (8 random images from each category). Images with blank backgrounds or incorrect masks were excluded.
    *   *Blur Condition:* Gaussian filter ($\sigma = 5$ pixels).

### Optimization and Implementation Details
*   **Principal Distortion Optimization:**
    *   **Method:** Projected gradient descent to maximize the variance of log sensitivity ratios across models.
    *   **Iterations:** 2500 iterations for standard comparisons; 500 iterations for ViT vs. EfficientNet.
    *   **Learning Rate:** Exponential decay starting at 10.0 and ending at 0.001.
    *   **Target Distortion Size ($\alpha$):** 0.1.
    *   **Constraints:** The perturbation $\epsilon$ was scaled at each step such that the image $\mathbf{s} + 1000\epsilon$ remained within the valid RGB pixel range [0, 1] to prevent clipping.
*   **FIM Calculation:** For deterministic models $f(\cdot)$, the FIM was calculated as $\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{s}) = \mathbf{J}_f(\mathbf{s})^\top \mathbf{J}_f(\mathbf{s})$, where $\mathbf{J}_f$ is the Jacobian.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

### Early Visual Models Analysis
*   **Distortion Separation:** The optimized principal distortions produced diverse log sensitivity ratios across the four models (LN, LG, LGG, LGN). In contrast, random distortions yielded ratios clustered near zero, failing to differentiate the models.
*   **Human Perceptual Alignment (Visual Inspection):**
    *   When principal distortions were rescaled so a specific model was equally sensitive to both, we observed the following regarding human visibility:
        *   **LGN Model:** Both rescaled distortions were visible to human observers.
        *   **LN Model:** Both rescaled distortions were visible to human observers.
        *   **LG Model:** The scaled $\epsilon_2$ distortion was not visible, while $\epsilon_1$ was immediately apparent (indicating a mismatch with human thresholds).
        *   **LGG Model:** The scaled $\epsilon_1$ distortion was not visible, while $\epsilon_2$ was apparent (indicating a mismatch).
    *   These observations suggest the LGN and LN models are closest to human distortion thresholds.

### Deep Neural Networks: Architecture Comparison (AlexNet vs. ResNet50)
*   **Separability:** Principal distortions reliably separated the models based on architecture.
*   **Hierarchical Structure:** Early layers of both architectures exhibited smaller log sensitivity ratios (closer in metric space), while late layers showed larger divergences.
*   **Texture vs. Smooth Regions:**
    *   **AlexNet Sensitivity ($\epsilon_1$):** We observed that AlexNet was consistently more sensitive to distortions concentrated on high-variability regions, such as texture or the foreground object.
    *   **ResNet50 Sensitivity ($\epsilon_2$):** We observed that ResNet50 was consistently more sensitive to distortions concentrated on relatively constant/smooth regions of the image (e.g., sky, smooth background).
*   **Consistency:** This distinction in local geometry (texture vs. smooth) was consistent across 100 base images and replicated across 3 randomly initialized instances of each architecture.
*   **Edge Artifacts:** In tests using images with blank centers or blank surrounds, AlexNet remained sensitive to the textured "stuff" regions, while ResNet50 remained sensitive to the blank/smooth regions.

### Deep Neural Networks: Training Data Comparison (ImageNet vs. Stylized ImageNet)
*   **Separation Driver:** When comparing standard ImageNet models against Stylized ImageNet (SIN) models for both architectures, the principal distortions separated the models by **architecture** (AlexNet vs. ResNet) rather than training dataset.
*   **Sensitivity Patterns:**
    *   Both Standard and SIN-trained AlexNet models remained more sensitive to high-variability/texture perturbations.
    *   Both Standard and SIN-trained ResNet50 models remained more sensitive to constant-area perturbations.

### Deep Neural Networks: Robustness Comparison (Standard vs. Adversarial Training)
*   **Separation Driver:** When comparing standard models against Adversarially Trained (AT) models, the principal distortions separated the models by **training type** rather than architecture.
*   **Sensitivity Patterns:**
    *   **Standard Models:** More sensitive to distortions appearing as unstructured noise.
    *   **Adversarially Trained Models:** More sensitive to distortions appearing as smooth color changes or shading around edges (low-frequency perturbations).
    *   This result contrasts sharply with the Stylized ImageNet experiment.

### Modern Architectures (EfficientNet vs. ViT)
*   **Separability:** Principal distortions reliably separated EfficientNet-B0 and ViT (Vision Transformer) layers.
*   **Artifacts:** The distortions for ViT ($\epsilon_2$) exhibited grid-like artifacts corresponding to the patch size of the input, distinct from the CNN distortions.

### Spatial Frequency Analysis (Blur Experiment)
*   **Method:** We applied low-pass filters to either the foreground or background of ImageNet-9 images.
*   **AlexNet:** The distortion to which AlexNet was most sensitive consistently concentrated on image regions with higher spatial frequencies (the non-blurred parts).
*   **ResNet50:** The distortion to which ResNet50 was most sensitive consistently concentrated on image regions with low-frequency information (the blurred parts), regardless of whether the blur was in the foreground or background.

The eigenvectors of the FIM (ϵ1, ϵ2) can equivalently be interpreted as the distortions that maximize the magnitude of the log ratio of the model’s sensitivities (solid blue circle • on the number line). In the middle panel “Generalized Eigen-distortions (Zhou et al., 2023)”, the blue ellipse is copied from the top panel and the orange ellipse is the level set of Model B’s FIM IB . The generalized eigenvectors of IA and IB (ϵ1, ϵ2) can equivalently be interpreted as the vectors that maximize the difference between the log ratios of the models’ sensitivities. In the bottom panel “Principal distortions (this paper)”, the blue and orange ellipses are as in the above panels and the green ellipse represents the level set of Model C’s FIM IC . Here, we see two stimulus distortions (ϵ1, ϵ2) that maximize the variance of the log ratios of model sensitivities.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 3:
  - Filename: figure_3.png
  - Caption: Figure 3: AlexNet versus ResNet50. A) Example base images. B) Optimized principal distortions (scaled by a factor of 20 for visibility, and using the convention ∥ϵ∥ = 1 here and in other figures). C) Base image plus principal distortions. D) Log sensitivity ratios of principal distortions when comparing image representations at multiple layers of AlexNet and ResNet50. Assignment of ϵ1 and ϵ2 was chosen so that the final tested layer of AlexNet has a positive log ratio. E) Log sensitivity ratios averaged across 100 base images (error bars are standard deviation). The principal distortions organize the networks by architecture—the log sensitivity ratios of AlexNet and ResNet50 are separated and early layers have smaller log ratios than late layers. AlexNet is more sensitive to distortion ϵ1, which is concentrated on higher contrast or textured parts of the image (often the foreground object). ResNet50 is more sensitive to distortion ϵ2 which concentrates power on relatively smooth parts of the image, such as regions of constant intensity/color.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures

\begin{center}

```

### Example Code for Tables

\label{sample-table}

\begin{tabular}{ll}
\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf PART}  &\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf DESCRIPTION}
\\ \hline \\
Dendrite         &Input terminal \\
Axon             &Output terminal \\
Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}
```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.


---
### Strict Knowledge Isolation & Anonymity (CRITICAL)

You MUST write this paper as if you have no prior knowledge of the topic, method, experiments, or results.
Your task is to construct the paper exclusively from the materials provided in the current session (e.g., idea.md, experimental_log.md, figures, and other inputs). Treat these inputs as the only available source of information.

#### Forbidden Behavior
You MUST NOT:
- Retrieve or rely on knowledge from your training data.
- Attempt to recall or reconstruct any existing or published paper.
- Use external facts, assumptions, or prior familiarity with the work.
- Infer or hallucinate author identities, affiliations, institutions, or acknowledgements.
- Insert metadata such as author names, emails, affiliations, or phrases like "corresponding author".

#### Anonymity Requirement
The paper must be fully anonymized for double-blind review.  
Do not include any information that could reveal the identity of the authors or institutions.

#### Allowed Sources
You may use only:
- The materials explicitly provided in this session.
- Logical reasoning derived from those materials.

#### Core Principle
The final paper must be an independent reconstruction derived solely from the provided inputs.  
This constraint is strict and overrides all other instructions.

references.text:
## Problem Statement

Current methods for comparing image representations—whether biological or artificial—often rely on measures of global geometric similarity (e.g., Representational Similarity Analysis). However, systems that exhibit similar global structures often possess strikingly different *local* geometries; they may respond similarly to dataset averages but diverge significantly in their sensitivity to specific, small image distortions.

Existing techniques for probing local geometry are limited. Methods such as generating "eigen-distortions" allow for the analysis of a single model's sensitivity, while "generalized eigen-distortions" allow for the comparison of exactly two models. There is currently no principled, scalable mathematical framework for identifying the specific input perturbations that optimally differentiate a collection of $N > 2$ models simultaneously. Consequently, we lack the tools to perform dimensionality reduction on the space of model sensitivities, making it difficult to visualize and interpret exactly how multiple complex architectures differ in their local processing of visual information.

## Core Hypothesis

We hypothesize that we can optimally differentiate a set of $N$ image representations by treating their local sensitivities as points in a metric space derived from the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM).

We propose to develop a method called **"Principal Distortions."** Analogous to Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which finds directions of maximal variance in data, our method will synthesize specific image distortions that maximize the *variance* of the models' sensitivities under a novel local geometric metric. By optimizing for these distortions, we will generate a compact set of stimuli that reveals the most significant dimensions of disagreement across the entire population of models, without requiring ground truth labels or extensive datasets.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Modeling Local Information Geometry
We will rigorously quantify the local geometry of any stochastic image representation using the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM). Let an image representation define a conditional density $p(\mathbf{r} | \mathbf{s})$, where $\mathbf{s}$ is a $K$-dimensional vector of image pixels and $\mathbf{r}$ is the response vector.

We will define the FIM, $\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{s})$, at a base image $\mathbf{s}$ as:
$$ \mathbf{I}(\mathbf{s}) := \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{r} \sim p(\mathbf{r}|\mathbf{s})} \left[ \nabla_{\mathbf{s}} \log p(\mathbf{r}|\mathbf{s}) \nabla_{\mathbf{s}} \log p(\mathbf{r}|\mathbf{s})^\top \right] $$

For deterministic Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) with output mapping $f(\mathbf{s})$, we will formulate the local geometry by assuming the output is corrupted by additive Gaussian noise with covariance $\mathbf{\Sigma}$. In this formulation, the FIM becomes a function of the model Jacobian $\mathbf{J}_f(\mathbf{s})$:
$$ \mathbf{I}(\mathbf{s}) = \mathbf{J}_f(\mathbf{s})^\top \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{J}_f(\mathbf{s}) $$

We will define the **sensitivity** of a model to a specific distortion vector $\epsilon$ in the image space as the distance induced by the Fisher-Rao metric:
$$ d(\mathbf{s}; \epsilon) := \sqrt{\epsilon^\top \mathbf{I}(\mathbf{s}) \epsilon} $$

### 2. Defining a Metric for Model Comparison
To compare models, we require a metric that is invariant to trivial scaling of the FIMs (which corresponds to global sensitivity gain) and permutation of distortions. We will define a pairwise metric between two models, $A$ and $B$, evaluated at two distortion directions $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$:

$$ m_{\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}}(\mathbf{I}_A, \mathbf{I}_B) := \left| \log \frac{d_A(\mathbf{u})}{d_A(\mathbf{v})} - \log \frac{d_B(\mathbf{u})}{d_B(\mathbf{v})} \right| $$

This metric captures the difference in the log-ratios of sensitivities, effectively normalizing out the global scale of each model's response.

### 3. Synthesizing Principal Distortions
Our core algorithmic contribution will be the generalization of this metric to $N > 2$ models. We will search for a pair of distortions $\{\epsilon_1, \epsilon_2\}$ that maximizes the sum of squared pairwise distances between all models in the set.

We formulate the optimization objective as maximizing the **variance** of the models' log sensitivity ratios:

$$ \{\epsilon_1, \epsilon_2\} = \underset{\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}}{\arg\max} \sum_{n=1}^N \left| \log \frac{d_{A_n}(\mathbf{u})}{d_{A_n}(\mathbf{v})} - \frac{1}{N} \sum_{m=1}^N \log \frac{d_{A_m}(\mathbf{u})}{d_{A_m}(\mathbf{v})} \right|^2 $$

Here, $d_{A_n}(\mathbf{u})$ represents the sensitivity of the $n$-th model to distortion $\mathbf{u}$.

### 4. Optimization Algorithm
We will solve this maximization problem using **Projected Gradient Descent**. We will compute the gradients of the objective function $L(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})$ with respect to the distortions.

The gradient with respect to $\mathbf{u}$ will be implemented as:
$$ \nabla_{\mathbf{u}} L(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum_{n=1}^N \left\{ \log \frac{d_n^2(\mathbf{u})}{d_n^2(\mathbf{v})} - \frac{1}{N} \sum_{m=1}^N \log \frac{d_m^2(\mathbf{u})}{d_m^2(\mathbf{v})} \right\} \left\{ \frac{\mathbf{I}_n(\mathbf{s})\mathbf{u}}{d_n^2(\mathbf{u})} - \frac{1}{N} \sum_{m=1}^N \frac{\mathbf{I}_m(\mathbf{s})\mathbf{u}}{d_m^2(\mathbf{u})} \right\} $$

The gradient for $\mathbf{v}$ follows a symmetric derivation. We will iteratively update $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ using these gradients and project them onto a sphere of fixed norm $\alpha$ to constrain the distortion magnitude.

The algorithm will proceed as follows:
1.  **Input:** $N$ pre-trained models (defining matrices $\mathbf{I}_1, \dots, \mathbf{I}_N$), base image $\mathbf{s}$.
2.  **Initialize:** Random vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}$.
3.  **Loop:**
    *   Compute sensitivities $d_n(\mathbf{u})$ and Jacobian-vector products $\mathbf{I}_n \mathbf{u}$.
    *   Compute the log-ratio residuals relative to the mean across models.
    *   Update $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ via gradient ascent.
    *   Normalize $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ to target norm $\alpha$.
4.  **Output:** The principal distortions $\{\epsilon_1, \epsilon_2\}$.

## Expected Contribution

1.  **Theoretical Framework:** We will provide a rigorous mathematical foundation for comparing the local geometry of multiple representations simultaneously, extending concepts from information geometry (Fisher-Rao metric) to multi-model comparison.
2.  **Dimensionality Reduction for Model Differences:** This work will introduce "Principal Distortions" as a dimensionality reduction technique. Just as PCA identifies variance in data, our method will identify variance in *model mechanisms*, allowing researchers to visualize the primary axes along which complex models diverge.
3.  **Efficient Model Probing:** This framework will enable the synthesis of optimal stimuli that differentiate a large set of models using only a minimal number of queries (distortions), significantly improving upon the efficiency of pairwise comparison methods (which scale quadratically with $N$).
4.  **Interpretability:** By visualizing the synthesized distortions, we expect to reveal qualitative differences in how models process information (e.g., sensitivity to texture vs. shape, or high vs. low frequency content) that are currently obscured by global similarity metrics.

notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
